messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 53
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Airline Pilot
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Affective Expression: Crying, Crowding: Crowded places, Moral Violation: People misbehaving
  Threat: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind., Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mateo traces the steel deadbolt with his thumb for the third time, a ritual he performs every night before his wife, Leilani, comes to bed. At fifty-three, he is a senior pilot with an impeccable record, a man who commands a Boeing 777 with quiet authority, yet he cannot trust a simple lock to do its job. He moves from the front door to the back, then checks the windows, one by one. To him, the unusual quiet of their suburban home at night is not peaceful; it is a vacuum waiting to be filled with danger. He has come to believe that silence is the sound of something terrible gathering itself just out of sight.

It has been eighteen months since the layover that changed everything. Detained on baseless espionage charges in a country with a notoriously brutal security apparatus, Mateo spent three weeks in a cell built for six that held twenty. The trauma does not live in his mind as a continuous film, but as a series of stark, still photographs. There is the guard’s bored, cruel face, illuminated by a bare bulb. There is the image of an older man in the corner, shoulders shaking with silent sobs. There is the grimy wall, inches from his face, where he spent hours trying to disappear. When these memories surface, they are not just visual. The air in his lungs will suddenly seem to thicken, and he can smell the cloying odour of unwashed bodies and harsh disinfectant that permeated the cell. The wave of panic and despair that follows is so absolute, so physically overwhelming, that he has to brace himself against a wall or sit down until it passes.

These intrusions are no longer random. His world has become a landscape of hidden triggers. As a pilot, he must navigate the very environments that now torment him. The airport terminal, once a familiar workspace, is now a gantlet. He finds himself constantly scanning the faces in the crowd, watching other people’s hands and eyes for any sign of aggression or ill intent. He is certain that danger is everywhere, and he is the only one vigilant enough to see it. A few months ago, waiting to board a flight, a toddler began to wail. The sound of that child's crying—high-pitched and helpless—transported him instantly back to the cell, to the chorus of weeping men he could do nothing to help. The smell of bleach and sweat filled his nostrils, and he had to retreat to a bathroom stall, gripping the cold metal partition until the ‘photograph’ of the sobbing man in his mind finally faded.

The most difficult trigger is what he thinks of as ‘disorder.’ Any public display of misbehaviour—teenagers shoving each other, a passenger arguing heatedly with a gate agent—ignites a profound sense of dread. It reminds him of the guards, of how their casual cruelty was a form of entertainment, a violation of the basic order that should govern how people treat one another. He has come to see these smaller infractions as proof that the world is fundamentally unsafe and chaotic, that the veneer of civilization is thin and easily torn.

This constant state of high alert has taken its toll. He has started calling in sick for flights to certain regions, unable to face the possibility of being trapped so far from home again. Leilani knows something is wrong; she sees him checking the locks, sees the haunted look in his eyes when a loud noise breaks the evening quiet, but he cannot bring himself to give her the details. The shame is too great. The breaking point came last week, during a routine approach into San Francisco. For a split second, lost in a memory, he felt the cockpit shrink around him, the instrument panel blurring into the grimy wall of the cell. His co-pilot’s voice snapped him back. It was that moment of disconnection, the realization that he was becoming a danger in the one place he had always felt in control, that finally drove him to seek help. He is terrified of losing his wings, but what frightens him more is the thought of staying trapped in those mental photographs forever.
